look_here_first: ANNUAL BEARDGRASS / RABBIT'S-FOOT GRASS: in damp ditches and disturbed soils look for a short-to-medium ANNUAL grass with a dense, soft, pale-green to tawny cylindrical or lobed flowerhead. The fluffy HALO comes chiefly from TWO long awns (typically 4–10 mm) arising from notched tips of the TWO GLUMES around each tiny one-flowered spikelet. The much smaller fertile lemma can ALSO bear a short awn: NEVER teach 'glumes awned, lemma always awnless.' Separate introduced Setaria by bristle origin (sterile branchlets beneath spikelets), and Carolina Phalaris by compact firm glumes without this long awn halo.

best_field_traits: Introduced cool-season annual; 5–65(–100) cm tall, tufted or ascending and sometimes rooting at low nodes, broadly green grass in disturbed wet fields, pond margins or ditches.
Very densely contracted pale-green to yellow-brown panicle (about 1–17 cm), cylindrical, narrowly ellipsoid or irregularly lobed; soft fuzzy impression from numerous awns.

Each spikelet is one-flowered, about 1–2.7 mm glumes; two glume tips each slightly notched and each carrying conspicuous 4–10 mm fine awn; the awns belong to the glumes, not a Setaria-type sterile branchlet.
Fertile lemma tiny (~0.5–1.5 mm), usually with its own much shorter awn (~0.5–1 mm, sometimes longer or missing)—not the long halo seen on the whole head.
Leaf ligule membranous (~2.5–16 mm), upper sheaths sometimes inflated; not adequately resolved in current public lesson photo.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: CRITICAL: isolated mature P. monspeliensis spikelet front + edge at 10–20× with mm ruler showing TWO notched glumes and each 4–10 mm glume awn traced to actual insertion
Open same spikelet to show ONE tiny fertile floret, short lemma and any short lemma awn; be sure not to confuse lemmas with the two longer glumes
Scaled transparent membranous ligule in fresh true blade/sheath collar
Fully rooted annual fibrous base plus culm nodes photographed on same verified specimen
Matched Setaria parviflora bristles FROM sterile branchlets and P. viridis AWNLESS glumes; no arrow without a visible attachment structure
crew_field_check: FIRST—head: softly fuzzy or rabbit-foot-like compact green to straw-colored narrowly ellipsoid/cylindrical panicle; sometimes branched lobes, not necessarily one uniform straight cylinder.
SECOND—annual base: tufted/ascending slender culms with fibrous roots, often in moist soil; do not infer rooted annual anatomy from cropped seedhead photos.

THIRD—one ACTUAL mature spikelet at 10–20×: TWO narrow glumes, each with a notch and a long slender awn from the notch, usually 4–10 mm. Hair/awn origin must be traced from the base, not guessed from the outside halo.

FOURTH—inside those glumes: ONE fertile floret; the much shorter shiny lemma often has its own much shorter awn, sometimes apparently awnless depending on specimen; never call the long outer hair a lemma awn from the group photo.
FIFTH—true leaf collar: a translucent MEMBRANOUS ligule typically several mm long, not a Setaria hair-fringed ligule; capture a scaled true sheath/blade junction.

SIXTH—check introduced look-alikes: P. viridis (generally awnless glumes and creeping/perennial), Setaria spp. (bristles from sterile branches rather than two paired glumes), Phleum pratense (shorter glume awns), Phalaris caroliniana (firm broad keeled scales, no long fuzzy halo) and Alopecurus spp. (shorter/absent glume awns; often lemma-awns).

comparisons.key_distinctions: Phalaris caroliniana: firm smooth-sided head of overlapping broad strongly keeled glumes, WITHOUT Polypogon's halo of long fine awns. Setaria parviflora/foxtails: bristles arise from modified sterile BRANCHES beneath spikelets, unlike TWO long AWNS attached to notched Polypogon GLUMES; Setaria also has hair-fringed ligule. Polypogon viridis: related grass without long awns on glumes, often creeping perennial. Phleum pratense: much shorter glume awns, lemma unawned, dense firmer timothy head. Alopecurus: often a short lemma awn, usually glumes without the conspicuous paired long awns of P. monspeliensis. Examine attachment, not mere fuzzy color.

grass_species_finalization_20261024.priority: Species confirmation by ONE measured mature spikelet, not the soft rabbit-foot seedhead silhouette.
grass_species_finalization_20261024.look_here_first: In a moist disturbed site, look for an annual tuft bearing a very dense pale-green/tawny, often lobed bottlebrush panicle. At 10–20×, trace TWO long awns to the shallowly notched tips of TWO glumes around ONE fertile floret. The inner lemma is much shorter and may itself carry a short, fragile awn.
crew_steps: 1. Photograph the WHOLE rooted tuft and full attached panicle; note whether culms are upright or bent/rooting at lower nodes. Do not infer annual roots from a detached head.
2. Photograph the TRUE blade–sheath junction. The ligule is a translucent membrane, not a Setaria-type hair fringe; measure from membrane base to free edge.

3. On one mature intact spikelet, measure the body separately from its long awns. GrassBase: spikelet 2–3 mm EXCLUDING awns; the two one-veined, keeled glumes are similar and exceed the single fertile floret.

4. Follow EACH 4–7 mm GrassBase glume awn to the notch (sinus) at the tip of its OWN glume. Both glume margins are minutely ciliate and the surfaces can be rough; do not draw an insertion-point arrow unless actual pixels resolve it.

5. Open that same spikelet: one fertile lemma about 1–1.5 mm, hyaline and five-veined (lateral veins subtle), with a toothed tip and OPTIONAL separate 0–2 mm awn; palea about lemma length. Never teach the fertile lemma as obligatorily awnless.

6. Compare local fuzzy-head look-alikes by bristle origin: Setaria bristles are sterile branchlets BELOW spikelets, whereas Polypogon has awns ON glumes. Phalaris caroliniana has firm pointed glumes without this paired long-glume-awn halo. P. viridis generally lacks these conspicuous glume awns.
7. Stop at a provisional field ID if the glume notch, glume pair, and fertile lemma cannot be seen. Do not claim microscopic verification from existing wide or seedhead-only photographs.

published_measurements.growth: Annual; culms about 6–80 cm, tufted or solitary, sometimes bent at lower nodes (Kew GrassBase).
published_measurements.panicle: Dense spike-like branched panicle about 1.5–16 cm long and 1–3.5 cm wide, sometimes lobed (Kew GrassBase).
published_measurements.ligule: Membranous, 3–15 mm in Kew GrassBase; 2.5–16 mm in Go Botany. Photograph free membrane edge at 1-mm scale.
published_measurements.spikelet: 2–3 mm EXCLUDING glume awns; one fertile floret, laterally compressed; may fall entire with tiny pedicel piece (Kew).
published_measurements.glumes: Two similar one-veined, keeled glumes, notched at tips; each bears a 4–7 mm awn (Kew); broader 4–10 mm in Go Botany.
published_measurements.lemma: Fertile lemma 1–1.5 mm, hyaline, five-veined with subtle lateral veins and dentate/four-toothed tip; awn absent or 0–2 mm (Kew).
published_measurements.palea: Approximately as long as fertile lemma; hyaline and two-veined (Kew).
published_measurements.caution: Measurements above are published treatment values, not verified from current installed images. Keep awn length OUT of the spikelet-body measurement; avoid treating one regional ligule/lemma-awn range as an absolute cutoff.
